description: Test your knowledge of PA H10 | Hemostasis & Bleeding Disorders.

cards.text: Define hemostasis and name its three overlapping components.
cards.answer: Hemostasis is the physiological process that stops bleeding after vascular injury while keeping blood fluid in intact vessels. Its three components are: (1) primary hemostasis (vascular response + platelet plug, seconds to 3 minutes), (2) secondary hemostasis (coagulation cascade → fibrin clot, minutes), and (3) fibrinolysis (clot dissolution, hours to days).

tip.tip: Remember the timeline: Platelets (seconds) → Coagulation (minutes) → Fibrinolysis (hours/days)

cards.text: What is the role of von Willebrand factor (vWF) in primary hemostasis? What disease pattern does its absence cause?
cards.answer: vWF bridges exposed collagen to platelet GPIb receptor, enabling platelet adhesion—especially critical at high shear stress in arterioles. Without vWF (von Willebrand disease), platelet adhesion fails, producing a mucocutaneous bleeding pattern identical to thrombocytopenia but with a normal platelet count.

tip.tip: vWF = the 'bridge' between collagen and GPIb. No vWF = no adhesion = bleeding despite normal platelets.

cards.text: Describe the sequence of platelet activation after adhesion.
cards.answer: After GPIb–vWF adhesion, platelets undergo shape change (disc → spiky sphere), degranulation (releasing ADP, TxA₂, fibrinogen, vWF from α and δ granules), and membrane phospholipid flip. ADP and TxA₂ amplify the response via positive feedback, recruiting more platelets.

tip.tip: Shape → Granule release → Amplification (ADP + TxA₂) = Activation cascade

cards.text: How does GPIIb/IIIa mediate platelet aggregation? Name two drugs that target this pathway.
cards.answer: GPIIb/IIIa receptors on activated platelets bind fibrinogen, which bridges adjacent platelets together, forming the platelet plug. Inside-out signaling from ADP/TxA₂ receptors activates this conformational change. Clopidogrel (ADP receptor blocker) and abciximab (GPIIb/IIIa blocker) inhibit aggregation.

tip.tip: GPIIb/IIIa + fibrinogen = platelet-to-platelet bridges. Clopidogrel blocks the signal; abciximab blocks the glue.

cards.text: Why does a single dose of aspirin block platelet function for 8–10 days, unlike other antiplatelet drugs?
cards.answer: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX), blocking thromboxane A₂ synthesis. Platelets lack a nucleus and cannot re-synthesize COX, so the blockade lasts for the entire platelet lifespan (8–10 days). Other antiplatelet drugs are reversible and have shorter durations.

tip.tip: Aspirin = irreversible COX inhibition. No nucleus = no recovery. Lifespan = duration of effect.

cards.text: What is the difference in timeline between primary hemostasis and secondary hemostasis?
cards.answer: Primary hemostasis (vascular response + platelet plug formation) occurs within seconds to 3 minutes. Secondary hemostasis (coagulation cascade → fibrin clot formation) takes minutes. The platelet plug is initially fragile and must be reinforced by fibrin from the coagulation cascade.

tip.tip: Primary = FAST (seconds), Secondary = SLOW (minutes). Platelets first, then fibrin reinforces.

cards.text: Name the vascular endothelium's three main anti-thrombotic mechanisms and their functions.
cards.answer: The normal endothelium is actively anti-thrombotic via: (1) prostacyclin (PGI₂) — inhibits platelet aggregation, (2) nitric oxide (NO) — inhibits platelet activation, and (3) tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) — promotes fibrinolysis. Vascular injury disrupts this, exposing pro-thrombotic subendothelium.

tip.tip: Intact endothelium = Anti-platelet + Anti-clot. Injured endothelium = Pro-coagulant collagen + vWF exposed.

cards.text: Clinically, what bleeding pattern distinguishes von Willebrand disease from thrombocytopenia, given that both present with mucocutaneous bleeding?
cards.answer: The key distinguishing feature is the platelet count: in von Willebrand disease, the platelet count is NORMAL (vWF deficiency impairs adhesion, not production), whereas in thrombocytopenia, the count is LOW. vWF disease typically shows prolonged bleeding time at high shear; thrombocytopenia shows global platelet dysfunction. Laboratory testing (aPTT, vWF levels, von Willebrand factor assay) confirms the diagnosis.

tip.tip: Same bleeding pattern, different platelet count. Normal count + mucocutaneous bleeding = think vWF, not thrombocytopenia.
